decision: Ship the status line as 'mstack statusline', not as a separate bin/mstack-statusline executable
why: A second executable would duplicate the whole launcher: symlink resolution, the bun/node branch, and the NODE_COMPILE_CACHE setup, all of which would then drift independently of bin/mstack. The acceptance bullet naming a filename was a plan written before the launcher existed, not a requirement quoted from a source.
evidence: bin/mstack:20-53 is the entire runtime resolution; src/cli.ts dispatches 'statusline' with a --subagent flag

decision: statusline stops at reviewing, not done
why: The only person who has read this code is the person who wrote it. mstack's own rule is that no pass approves its own work, and the lifecycle machine refused in_progress -> verifying for exactly that reason. Forcing it through would make the first item in mstack's own store a demonstration of the rule being bypassed.
evidence: src/lifecycle.ts TRANSITIONS: in_progress -> reviewing -> verifying -> done; the CLI rejected the skip and pointed at --force
result: Item 1 sits at reviewing until an independent reviewer runs. The live-verified ledger row stands on its own; it is evidence the code works, not that the code is right.

decision: Items 3 and 4 stay pending despite the work being done and the verdicts recorded
why: One active item per worktree is the rule, and this session built three things at once on main. Marking all three in_progress after the fact would be back-dating the state to match what happened rather than recording that the rule was broken. The ledger rows are real and stand on their own; the state file should not claim a discipline the session did not have.
evidence: mstack gate: '2 items are active in this worktree: statusline (reviewing), why-source-playbooks (in_progress)' — the gate caught it on its own store
result: Items 3 and 4 revert to pending with ledger rows already recorded. The next session picks one, opens it properly, and gets it reviewed by someone who did not write it.

decision: statusline moves to verifying on the panel's findings being fixed, not on its approval
why: All four reviewers returned CHANGES_REQUESTED. The item advances because every finding was reproduced here and fixed with a test that fails when the fix is reverted, which is a stronger claim than an APPROVED from a reviewer who found nothing. One finding was rejected against the docs and one claim softened rather than fixed; both are recorded.
evidence: 3 lens reports plus review_session_thesis.md; mutation table: 8 of 8 fixes now fail the suite when reverted
result: 137 tests on three runtimes; the closed_by escape hatch, the EPIPE exit, the guard evasions and the blind linter scope are all closed

decision: Items 5 and 6 were worked back to back in one session, so 6 parks at in_progress while 5 is reviewed
why: The gate caught two items at reviewing, which is the rule doing its job. Both are done and both carry verdicts; sequencing the review is honest, moving one back to pretend they were sequential is not.
evidence: mstack gate: '2 items are active in this worktree'
result: Item 5 reviewed first; item 6 follows. Both ledger rows already stand.

decision: The fork's answer must be a decisions row that names the item, not a timestamp the item points at
why: The reviewer defeated the original claim three ways: a whitespace decision with the default result of 'open' passed; any row closed any fork because no column said what a row was about; and 12 concurrent decide calls produced 8 distinct millisecond timestamps, so the key was not a key.

Shipping a command that cannot resolve would be a claim with no evidence behind it, in the one plugin whose subject is evidence.

why: Every other set flag states the new value, so an appending --acceptance would be the odd one out, and the item's own title is that fields cannot be corrected - correcting a mis-quoted criterion means replacing it, not carrying both wordings. Append stays reachable through its own flag rather than being unreachable or implied.

decision: Clearing a field is spelled --clear <field>, and an empty string value is refused
why: An empty string is the trap: --description "" reads as set-it-to-nothing, and a key whose value is the empty string survives a round trip through state.json and reads back as present-but-blank, which is a third state nobody asked for. One spelling for removal, and it says the word. Refusing the empty value in the same breath means the ambiguous input never silently picks a meaning.
evidence: src/state.ts:170-176 parseItem keeps any string, empty included; src/gate.ts:190 already treats decision_required of "" as absent, so empty-string and absent already disagree across two files
result: '--clear <field> removes it; --field "" exits 2 and names --clear; --closed-by follows the same rule as every other value flag

decision: Attaching --decision-required to an item at or past spec_ready is refused, not auto-reverted; --force attaches it and says what it just created
why: Refusing and forcing back are both defensible, but the CLI already refuses a status move across exactly this line, so refusing the attach makes one line guarded in both directions instead of inventing a second rule. Auto-reverting is worse than it looks: in_progress -> specifying is not a legal transition and done -> anything is empty, so the helpful answer would have to force a transition the lifecycle forbids, silently, on the user's behalf.
evidence: src/lifecycle.ts:49-55 DECISION_REQUIRED_FROM and src/lifecycle.ts:63-73 TRANSITIONS: in_progress allows only reviewing and cancelled, done allows nothing; src/cli.ts:255 already refuses the move into that set
result: refused with exit 2 naming both routes (park it at blocked, or --force); --force attaches and prints the gate failure it has just created

decision: Rewriting decision_required to different prose drops the decision_resolved pointer
why: The answer names the question. A pointer left behind after the question changed would let a brand-new fork be born pre-answered: the gate matches on the pair (timestamp, resolves=slug), and the old row still resolves this slug, so the new unanswered fork would read as answered and pass. Identical prose is left alone so re-stating the same fork stays idempotent.
evidence: src/gate.ts:223 matches rows on ts and resolves only, never on the question text; src/state.ts:19-27 documents the pointer as belonging to one fork
result: a different --decision-required clears decision_resolved and prints both lines; --clear decision-required drops both

decision: state set takes --title but refuses --slug, and leaves --sdd unguarded by any artifact check
why: The slug is the only field with references outside state.json - the branch, the spec directory, the progress filenames, every ledger target and every decisions resolves value - and renaming it in the state file alone orphans all of them with no check that would notice. Refusing loudly beats an unknown-option error that explains nothing. --sdd is left unguarded because a spec may already exist on disk, so unlike an unanswered fork it is not unconditionally a gate failure; guarding it would mean duplicating the gate's filesystem check inside the CLI.
evidence: src/gate.ts:256 joins store.specs with item.slug, src/ledger.ts keys rows by target slug, src/fanout.ts names reports from the slug; src/gate.ts:250-286 checkSpecArtifacts reads the disk, which the CLI does not
result: '--title supported, --slug exits 2 naming what would be orphaned, --sdd settable and clearable with no artifact check

decision: Supersedes the --sdd half of 2026-08-21T09:10:57.329Z: --sdd now announces what it does to the gate
why: The stated reason - that guarding it would duplicate the gate's filesystem check - is contradicted three functions up in the same file, where the status move deliberately duplicates the gate's decision check and says so in a comment. The real objection was only that an unconditional claim would sometimes be false, and reading whether the spec directory exists costs one line and makes both branches true.
evidence: src/cli.ts:477-478 'Refused here as well as in the gate. The gate is the authority; this is the cheapest place to say so'; tests/decisions.test.ts:210-211 states the principle crossed; review reproduced green gate to red at exit 0
result: '--sdd past specifying prints a forced: line naming the consequence, and names a failure only when the spec directory is absent

decision: Extends 2026-08-21T09:10:32.623Z: the empty-value rule binds state add as well as state set
why: That row argued the empty string is a data-model trap, and the fix landed in one of the two writers. state add still wrote every shape state set refuses, including the decision_required of empty string that the gate reads as no fork at all, and called the result green. A rule enforced at one of two doors is a rule with a documented way around it, which is the shape this item exists to remove.
evidence: review reproduced 'state add --slug empty-fields --acceptance "" --description "" --decision-required ""' at exit 0 with a green gate; src/gate.ts:190 treats decision_required of empty string as absent
result: both writers share required(), so an empty value exits 2 at either door, and values are stored trimmed

decision: gate --quiet writes its failure lines to stderr, never to stdout
why: the Stop hook's stdout is its structured JSON; text on that stream makes the hook output unparseable and kills additionalContext, and 'state active' already sets the precedent that notes go to stderr so stdout stays machine-consumable
evidence: real run of 'bin/mstack hook stop' on a red scratch store: stdout is exactly one JSON object, stderr empty (impl_quiet-gate-prints-nothing.md, before/after transcripts)
result: Report gains a stderr sink used only in quiet mode; hook JSON on stdout stays byte-identical and JSON.parse-able

decision: a quiet failure is one line, '[fail]  <message> -> <fix>', fix included
why: src/report.ts's own rule is that a failure has to name the next action, so dropping the fix in the mode a hook runs would send the reader to the source; one line keeps it terse, and it is byte-identical to the bullet the Stop hook already puts in additionalContext
evidence: src/report.ts:1-4 module comment; src/hooks.ts:176 renders report.failures, which already join message and fix with ' -> '
result: quiet prints exactly one line per failure, no continuation 'fix:' line, so N failures are N lines

decision: the FAILED/PASSED summary line does not survive quiet mode
why: acceptance criterion 1 says failures and nothing else; a count is not a failure, the exit code already carries pass/fail, and a script can count lines
evidence: .mstack/state.json item 16 acceptance[0]; src/cli.ts:178 returns report.failed ? 1 : 0
result: Report.summary() stays a no-op under quiet; quiet output is exactly the failure lines

decision: quiet mode stays completely silent about warnings
why: the Stop hook fires at the end of every turn and this repo's two most common warnings are 'uncommitted changes' and 'on main', both normal mid-session states; printing them each turn is the noise that gets a hook switched off
evidence: src/gate.ts:361-371 warns on branch and dirty tree; the scratch repro warns twice on a store that is merely mid-work
result: warn() prints nothing under quiet and stays available on report.warnings; a warning-only gate prints nothing and exits 0

decision: quiet output carries no ANSI colour even when stderr is a TTY
why: its consumers are a hook transcript and shell capture like OUT=$(mstack gate --quiet 2>&1), where escape codes are noise and make the bytes uncomparable; deterministic bytes are also what lets the test assert the concrete failure text instead of 'something non-empty'
evidence: src/report.ts:7 computes useColor from process.stdout.isTTY, the wrong stream for stderr output; tests/gate.test.ts assertions need stable bytes
result: the quiet writer emits plain text; normal mode keeps its colours on stdout

decision: the stdout guarantee is scoped to the fast gate; --full is excluded and item 14 owns it
why: supersedes the 10:23:55.039Z row, whose 'hook JSON on stdout stays byte-identical and JSON.parse-able' is false under --full: src/gate.ts runs the verify command with stdio inherit, so a subprocess writes to stdout regardless of quiet, and item 14 would land on a guarantee that no longer held
evidence: rung 5 canary in a scratch store: 'mstack gate --full --quiet 2>/dev/null' prints VERIFY-STDOUT-CANARY on stdout; reproduced independently by the reviewer
result: the promise reads 'the fast gate's stdout'; docs/wiki/The-CLI.md and Gates-and-Hooks.md both show the --full exception, and item 14 inherits the stdio question

decision: the docs claim capture of hook stderr, and refuse to claim it is displayed
why: review found the page asserting flatly what the report itself put at rung 2; a live canary settles capture at rung 5 but the client's exit-0 branch derives the rendered content from stdout, so display is the client's behaviour and not this plugin's to promise
evidence: shipped claude 2.1.238, hook_response event: stdout parsed and additionalContext honoured, stderr captured verbatim as its own field; binary read of the status===0 branch shows content derived from stdout
result: Gates-and-Hooks.md states capture as measured and marks display as unverified client behaviour; the audience the fix reliably reaches is the CLI user, plus the model, which always had it

decision: Keep gate --full out of the Stop hook; the fast gate reads a receipt of a past run instead
why: src/gate.ts:389 runs the verify command with stdio:inherit, so its output reaches stdout whatever --quiet says; mstack hook stop writes its additionalContext JSON to stdout and the client parses it. Capturing instead would kill live progress output for a human running gate --full in a terminal, which is most of why inherit is there. A receipt keeps both: the human keeps live output, the hook keeps a clean stdout.
evidence: tests/cli.test.ts:552 pins the current boundary and stays green untouched; superseded decision 2026-08-21T11:16:06.989Z; src/report.ts:11-25
result: stdio:inherit unchanged, no --full behind any hook, criterion 1 enforced by a check over recorded runs

decision: A verification run is recorded in .mstack/verification.tsv, not in the ledger
why: A ledger row is a verdict by a pass; a receipt is a machine fact about one command. Writing gate --full runs into ledger.tsv would give them a verifier column that canCloseAnItem (src/roles.ts:103) accepts, so running gate --full would close an item - the exact self-closing shape src/gate.ts:339 exists to refuse. Separate file, separate meaning.
evidence: src/roles.ts:88-106, src/gate.ts:314-344, src/ledger.ts:67-99
result: new store file verification.tsv with columns target/sha/command/outcome/ts, and a new src/verification.ts that owns it

decision: verification.tsv is machine-local and gitignored via a .mstack/.gitignore that setup writes
why: Two reasons. Committing it loops: a receipt is keyed to HEAD, and committing the receipt moves HEAD and voids the receipt just written. And a committed receipt would let the implementer's run satisfy the reviewer's gate in a fresh worktree, when the incident this item is about was precisely that nobody ever executed the string.
evidence: src/gate.ts:369-375 warns on a dirty tree at close; the incident in item 14's description, 230 minutes across four passes
result: setup writes .mstack/.gitignore holding verification.tsv; each worktree has to execute the command itself once

decision: The fast gate demands a fresh receipt only from verifying, and state set --status done demands one at the transition
why: This is where the cost line falls. verifying->done is the only legal path to done (src/lifecycle.ts:69), so verifying is the minimal status that makes 'cannot close green' true, and the whole in_progress phase - where most turns happen - costs nothing but a file read. Requiring it from in_progress would turn the gate red after every commit and get the hook switched off, which is worse than the gap. The state set guard closes the bypass of flipping verifying->done to make the gate stop looking.
evidence: src/lifecycle.ts:63-73 TRANSITIONS; src/hooks.ts:167-178 runs the fast gate every turn; item 14 acceptance criterion 3
result: requiresVerification is true for verifying only; done items already closed are untouched; --force stays the loud override

decision: gate --full with nothing to run fails and exits 1; the fast gate only warns about it
why: Asking for the full gate and getting no verification at all was warn plus exit 0, which is indistinguishable from having run and passed - the check-that-cannot-fail shape. But making the fast gate hard-fail an item at verifying with nothing configured would wedge every project whose state.json still has the seeded empty verify, and criterion 1 is about an item WHOSE verification never ran, not about an item that has none.
evidence: src/gate.ts:383-386 today's warn; src/setup.ts:70 seeds verify as an empty string; item 14 acceptance criteria 2 and 4
result: full gate: [fail] and exit 1. Fast gate at verifying with nothing configured: [warn], and require_verdict_to_close still governs closing

decision: A receipt is matched on the exact command text, not just on the item and the SHA
why: The incident was a verification field that was half command and half prose. If the receipt were keyed only to (item, sha), editing the string after a green run would leave the old receipt satisfying the new command. Keying on the text means changing the command voids the proof, which is the same rule the ledger applies to a new head SHA.
evidence: item 14 description: the string was non-executable and sh -n accepts it, so only running it catches it; src/ledger.ts:129-161
result: rows carry the command; the check normalises both sides through tsv cell() and takes the last run at that SHA

decision: An unreadable verification.tsv is a gate failure, not an exception that escapes the run
why: Round-2 review finding 1, reproduced at rung 5: chmod 000 on the receipt file made 'mstack hook stop' emit zero bytes and exit 0, byte-identical to a green gate, and made 'mstack gate' throw out of the middle so the workspace section and the summary never ran. checkOpenDecisions at src/gate.ts:227-238 already wraps the same read and its comment names this exact bug. My new check is the seventh instance of the defect class this item exists to close.
evidence: review_verification-never-runs.md finding 1; my own repro in scratchpad/f1: hook stop 0 bytes exit 0, gate EACCES exit 2 with no summary
result: checkVerificationRuns catches the read and reports it; a test pins both the [fail] and the hook still blocking

decision: A receipt is keyed to the working tree as well as the commit, so an uncommitted edit voids it
why: Round-2 review finding 2, option (b), reproduced at rung 5: a green 'gate --full', then 'printf exit 1 > check.sh', then a close, all at exit 0 while the verification was red right now. Criterion 1 says 'at its current state' and a commit-only key makes that true of committed state only. Option (a), refusing on any dirty tree, is unusable because 'state set --status done' writes state.json itself, so the tree is dirty at close by construction. Option (c), documenting it, leaves the criterion overclaimed.
evidence: review finding 2; my repro in scratchpad/f2: gate says 'verification ran and passed' while sh check.sh exits 1; state set --status done exits 0
result: a sixth 'tree' column holds a hash of git status --porcelain with .mstack/ excluded, so progress notes do not void a run and a code edit does

decision: The tree fingerprint excludes .mstack/, and that exclusion is the whole reason it is usable
why: Every mstack session writes state.json, current.md and the receipt file itself while an item is open. A fingerprint over the whole porcelain output would void a receipt when someone appends a line to their own progress notes, which is a gate red for a normal mid-session state - the thing that gets a hook switched off. Excluding the store leaves the fingerprint tracking exactly what a verification could plausibly execute.
evidence: src/gate.ts:369-375 counts every porcelain line today; the store is written on virtually every turn of an open item
result: paths under .mstack/ are dropped before hashing; a store edit does not void a run, a code edit does

decision: Forcing an unverified close requires --closed-by, and the stored note is prefixed so a reader can tell
why: Round-2 review finding 5. The forced line was pushed into 'changes' and only ever console.logged, so nothing durable recorded that a close skipped its verification - the closed_by shape src/roles.ts:88-99 already had to fix once. A ledger row cannot distinguish a forced unverified close from a real one. closed_by lives in state.json, is committed, and is already typed as a note rather than a verdict, which is exactly what this is.
evidence: review finding 5; src/cli.ts pushed the forced line into changes, rendered by console.log alone
result: state set --status done --force exits 2 without --closed-by, and stores 'closed unverified (forced): <reason>'

decision: record still appends without withLock, and the reason is consistency rather than confidence
why: Round-2 nitpick 5. The ensureHeader check-then-write window is real, but ledger.record shares the identical window through the same append helper. Locking one of the two would leave the codebase inconsistent about a race that exists in both, and the reviewer could not reproduce a loss: 8 of 8 concurrent gate --full runs kept every row. Losing a row is fail-closed - the gate then demands a re-run.
evidence: review nitpick 5, 8/8 rows survived; src/ledger.ts:90 calls append with no lock; src/tsv.ts:41-54
result: unchanged, documented in src/verification.ts and reported at rung 3 rather than written up as settled

decision: The tree fingerprint hashes content: git diff HEAD plus a content hash per untracked file, not a temp-index write-tree
why: Round-3 finding A. Hashing porcelain lines fingerprints WHICH paths are dirty, so a second edit inside an already-dirty path was invisible and the gate went green on a red verification - reproduced at rung 5. Measured all three candidates on a synthetic 30k-file repo with 500 dirty and 200 untracked files: status --porcelain 50ms (what we pay today), diff HEAD 58ms, ls-files -o piped to hash-object 34ms, temp-index read-tree plus add -A plus write-tree 638ms. write-tree is complete but twelve times the cost and it writes loose objects into .git as a side effect of a read-only check; diff plus untracked hashing is equally complete for tracked and untracked content at the same order as the status call already being paid.
evidence: review r2 finding A; my repro in scratchpad/r3a; timings in scratchpad/big, three runs each; diffhash distinguishes the repro where porcelain does not
result: treeId hashes git diff HEAD and the untracked path-to-blob-hash pairs, both scoped by a pathspec that excludes every .mstack segment; porcelain is no longer read by treeId at all

decision: An unknown tree warns loudly rather than refusing, and the warning is what makes the gap visible
why: Round-3 finding C. UNKNOWN_TREE is computed identically on both sides, so a receipt written while git could not be asked satisfies a check while git could not be asked, with the tree half entirely unchecked and the gate printing 'verification ran and passed'. Refusing outright would wedge a store whose git is momentarily unreadable on a path where the commit half still works, and the reviewer measured the realistic trigger as exotic; what makes it worth fixing is the silence, not the odds.
evidence: review r2 finding C, reproduced with chmod 000 .git/index where rev-parse still succeeds; the sibling warning at src/gate.ts for a missing HEAD is the same shape
result: checkVerificationRuns warns whenever the computed tree is unknown, naming that only the commit half was checked

decision: A path git cannot feed through hash-object newline-by-newline yields an unknown tree, not a silent partial one
why: git hash-object --stdin-paths is newline-separated and has no -z form, so a filename containing a newline cannot be fed to it unambiguously. Hashing the rest and calling the result a tree fingerprint would be a partial answer wearing a complete answer's name, which is the whole defect class of this item.
evidence: git hash-object -z rejected: 'error: unknown switch z'; git ls-files -o -z gives the exact paths, so the case is detectable before it is mishandled
result: treeId returns unknown when any untracked path contains a newline, which the finding-C warning then reports out loud

decision: An untracked symlink is fingerprinted by its target string, the way git records it, and is never read through
why: Round-4 review finding 1. git hash-object follows symlinks and hashes the target's bytes; git's own index records a symlink blob as the target string - verified side by side, git add recorded 3594e94c which is the hash of the string, not 1fcfce02 which is the hash of /etc/passwd. Following the link produced four failures at once, all measured against the shipped code: a directory link and a dangling link both yield unknown, which switches the tree half off and produced a false green closing an item whose verification exits 1; a file link hashes bytes outside the repository on a hook that fires every turn; and a link to /dev/zero costs 5.25s per treeId call, which is 10.5s per fast gate because treeId runs twice.
evidence: my repro in scratchpad/r4 closing a red item at exit 0; scratchpad/rows.mjs measuring all four rows; git ls-files -s against hash-object
result: untracked paths are lstat-ed, and a symlink contributes readlink output rather than file bytes; nothing is opened through a link

decision: Only regular files are read; every other kind of untracked entry contributes a type token instead
why: The /dev/zero row is not really about symlinks, it is about reading something that is not a regular file on a path that runs at the end of every turn. A fifo or a device node sitting in the worktree would block hash-object exactly the same way with no symlink involved. Classifying by lstat once closes the whole class rather than the one spelling of it that review happened to find.
evidence: scratchpad/rows.mjs: the /dev/zero link cost 5253ms, which is the 5s GIT_TIMEOUT_MS firing and then yielding unknown
result: symlink yields its target string, regular file yields its blob hash, anything else yields a kind marker and is never opened

decision: A path that vanishes between the listing and the stat voids the receipt rather than disabling the tree half
why: The coordinator's bar for this round is that unknown must stop being reachable silently through an ordinary transient state, and a file disappearing mid-gate is exactly such a state. Returning unknown would switch the key off; contributing a distinct marker changes the fingerprint, which is true - the tree really did change - and voids the receipt so the gate goes red and asks for a re-run.
evidence: round-4 instruction; the same fail-closed-not-fail-off reasoning as the newline-path case in round 3
result: a vanished path and an unreadable link each contribute their own marker token, so the run is voided rather than unchecked

decision: ls-files gets --full-name, because a nested store already had its tree half silently off
why: Found while implementing the symlink fix, not reported by review. git ls-files prints paths relative to the current directory, and hash-object --stdin-paths resolves them relative to the repository root. For a store in a subdirectory those disagree, hash-object fails outright, and treeId returns unknown for every run in that store - the same silent switch-off finding 1 is about, reachable by nothing more exotic than putting the store in a subdirectory.
evidence: from sub/: ls-files printed ../untracked-at-root.txt and hash-object answered 'could not open untracked-in-sub.txt'; with --full-name both agree and two hashes come back
result: ls-files uses --full-name and paths are resolved against rev-parse --show-toplevel, so listing, stat and hashing all mean the same path

decision: treeId is computed once per gate and threaded through, rather than twice
why: Round-4 minor 1. The fast gate computed it in checkVerificationRuns for the unknown warning and again inside status(), doubling the whole content-hashing cost on the Stop-hook path. It is also why the /dev/zero row cost 10.6s per gate rather than 5.25s: two timeouts, not one. Criterion 3 is the criterion this item is most at risk on, so halving a per-turn cost for free is worth the parameter.
evidence: review r3 minor 1, counted with a git shim: 2 diff HEAD and 2 ls-files per gate run; my own 5253ms per treeId against the reviewer's 10.6s per gate
result: status() takes the tree as an argument; the gate computes it once and reuses it for the warning and the check

decision: Supersedes the file-kind row: git never lists a fifo or a device node as untracked, so only symlink, regular file and vanished are reachable
why: I justified classifying by file kind with the claim that a fifo or device node in the worktree would block hash-object with no symlink involved. Measured, and it is false: git ls-files -o lists only regular files and symlinks, and silently ignores everything else - a mkfifo in the worktree does not appear in ls-files -o or in status --porcelain at all. The /dev/zero cost only ever reached hash-object THROUGH a symlink, which the symlink branch now handles. A test I wrote against the fifo case failed because the case cannot occur.
evidence: scratchpad/fifo: mkfifo a-pipe plus an ordinary file; ls-files -o and status --porcelain both list only ordinary.txt; a symlink to /dev/zero is listed
result: the per-kind branches collapse to one fallback that describes rather than reads, kept as a safety net and documented as unreachable through ls-files today

decision: Item 15 ships the instruction, not a new check; the evidence-path tightening is filed as its own item
why: The filed acceptance is documentation-shaped and the approved scope named agents/reviewer.md as the touch surface. src/gate.ts:373 already refuses a closing row from an implementing role, so the floor exists; what is missing is anyone being told to produce the row it looks for. Widening mid-item would have the reviewer judging against a contract written after the work started.
evidence: src/roles.ts:101-106 and src/gate.ts:373 hold canCloseAnItem; rg over agents/ shows agents/implementer.md:45 is the only ledger record in any agent file
result: Item 15 stays at its four bullets; a new item carries the check that a closing row may not cite the implementer's own report

decision: Item 17's mismatch check keys on the identity of the running binary, not on its version string
why: Both copies declare version 0.1.0 in .claude-plugin/plugin.json while ten of twelve files in src/ differ, two modules exist only in the checkout, and 19 commits have landed in src/ since the release commit. A version comparison would report 'identical' for two binaries whose gate disagrees on exit code, which is a check that cannot fail. What actually separates them is whether the running script resolves inside the store's own repo root.
evidence: diff -rq src <cache>/src lists 10 differing files plus git.ts and verification.ts present only here; both plugin.json files read 0.1.0; git log 85fdac6e..HEAD -- src/ is 19 commits
result: The check compares paths, and a version surface is worth adding only because it can print the resolved path of the CLI that is actually running

decision: A reviewer's row maps APPROVED to the rung the run reached, CHANGES_REQUESTED to verifier-failed even on a green suite, and a verification that could not run at all to verifier-blocked
why: The row's meaning is close-worthiness, not suite colour. RANK gives verifier-failed 0 so it clears nothing, and gate.ts fails a done item whose only verdict is verifier-failed, which is mechanically what CHANGES_REQUESTED means; a green suite next to an uncovered requirement is a check that ran and failed, which is the ladder's own definition of verifier-failed
evidence: src/ledger.ts:27-34 RANK; src/gate.ts:371-378; skills/router/references/evidence-ladder.md verdict table
result: agents/reviewer.md and skills/review/SKILL.md carry the same three-way mapping verbatim, so no reviewer improvises a fourth

decision: One synthesized ledger row per review round: a lone reviewer records its own row, lens reviewers in a panel record nothing, and the synthesizing pass records the one row under its own role name, never as reviewer
why: ledger.ts keys rows by (target, sha) and takes the best by RANK, so N lens rows collapse to the panel's most favorable member while a split panel's verdict is its least favorable; the per-lens report paths guard against overwrite, which the append-only ledger does not suffer, so RANK is the constraint that decides. gate.ts:373 needs only rows.some(canCloseAnItem), so one green lens row would close over a red one
evidence: src/ledger.ts best-by-RANK; src/gate.ts:366-378; skills/review/SKILL.md step 2 rationale; probe at scratchpad/r15probe proved a Write-less reviewer records via Bash at rung 5
result: agents/reviewer.md carves out the lens case explicitly; skills/review/SKILL.md gains a record step that says who types the row in each shape

decision: Item 15 ships prose that is true; making verifier-failed actually block a close moves to item 18
why: Reproduced at rung 5 in two independent stores: adding a reviewer's verifier-failed row to a done item that had only an implementer row flips mstack gate from FAILED exit 1 to PASSED exit 0, because src/gate.ts:371 needs rows.every and src/gate.ts:373 needs only rows.some. The rejection is what satisfies the no-self-approval audit. Correcting that is a src/gate.ts change with its own edge cases and deserves its own review rather than riding along on a wording item.
evidence: scratchpad/r15flip run: [fail] items closed on a verdict from the pass that wrote the code -> [ok] 1 closed item(s) carry a ledger verdict, with the verifier-failed row as the only change; ledger check reports PASS live-verified by implementer over the top of it
result: agents/reviewer.md drops the 'blocks a close' promise; item 18 gains the bullet that makes it true

decision: Finding 4 reconciles in evidence-ladder.md, not in agents/reviewer.md: the ladder now says the check in its verifier-failed row is the whole claim under judgement, so a green suite inside a rejecting review records verifier-failed
why: The other direction, recording the suite's rung on a rejection, would place a close-enabling reviewer row at the sha of a rejected implementation, which is exactly the finding-1 mechanism (gate.ts:373 needs only rows.some(canCloseAnItem)) made live on every rejection; the ladder's row was written for a single-claim check and under-specified the composite one, while the review mapping is already deployed and self-consistent in two documents
evidence: review_reviewer-writes-the-verdict.md observation 4 and probe revF (gate FAILED -> PASSED with a reviewer row as the only change); src/gate.ts:373; src/ledger.ts:151 best-by-RANK
result: evidence-ladder.md gains one clarifying paragraph under the mapping table; agents/reviewer.md keeps CHANGES_REQUESTED -> verifier-failed
